### Fig. 7: A monetary expansion with sticky wages

**Goal.** See how monetary policy can raise employment when nominal wages are sticky.

A monetary expansion, a lower fed funds rate, raises spending. In this example only wages are sticky, so the
other prices rise, from $P_0 = 1$ to $P' = 1.05$. With the nominal wage still at $\bar{W}$, the real wage
$\bar{W}/P'$ falls. At the lower real wage firms want more workers and fewer people want to work, so employment
rises from $A$ to $B$ and unemployment shrinks. This is the same function as in Fig. 6, now in period 1. Move
the period slider to 2 to let the nominal wage adjust.

```{python}
#| kind: widget
interact(sticky_wages,
         t=IntSlider(value=1, min=0, max=2, description="period t", style=WIDE),
         P_new=FloatSlider(value=1.05, min=1.0, max=1.25, step=0.05, description="new price level P′", style=WIDE),
         W_bar=FloatSlider(value=0.75, min=0.6, max=0.9, step=0.05, description="sticky nominal wage W̄", style=WIDE));
```

```{python}
#| kind: website
# @title Website version: Fig. 7 with a precomputed slider for the period
slider_figure(sticky_wages, "t", [0, 1, 2], start=1, label="period t")
```

**Source.** Adapted from Fig. 15.7 in Jones (2024), [*Macroeconomics*, 6th ed.](https://wwnorton.com/books/9781324063612)

**What to notice.**

- A 5 percent rise in prices lowers the real wage from 0.75 to 0.71 and raises employment from 0.70 to 0.81;
  unemployment falls from 0.42 to 0.26.
- The real wage and employment move in **opposite** directions. In actual business cycles, booms do not usually
  come with low real wages, so sticky wages alone cannot be the whole story of how monetary policy works.
- In period 2 the nominal wage has caught up with prices, the real wage is back at 0.67 and the market clears:
  in the long run, money does not change employment (the classical dichotomy).

### Fig. 8: A monetary expansion with sticky prices

**Goal.** See why, with sticky prices, labor demand is vertical and a monetary expansion raises both employment
and the real wage.

Now wages are flexible, but firms change their prices only slowly. At its sticky price, each firm agrees to
supply whatever customers demand. So spending decides output $Y$, and the production function decides how much
labor firms must hire to produce it (equation 9):

$$Y = \bar{A}K^{1/3}L^{2/3} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad L = \left(\frac{Y}{\bar{A}K^{1/3}}\right)^{3/2}.$$

Labor demand no longer depends on the wage: it is a **vertical** line. We start from the flexible-price output
$Y_0 = 1$, so point $A$ is the baseline. A monetary expansion raises the output demanded to $Y' = 1.15$, labor
demand shifts right, and to attract the extra workers the nominal wage must rise. With prices stuck, the real wage
$W/P$ rises too: the economy moves up along the labor supply curve to $B$.

```{python}
Y0 = 1.0          # output demanded before the shock: the flexible-price output of the baseline


def add_vertical(fig, L, label, color, dash="solid"):
    """A vertical labor demand curve at L (sticky prices), labelled just above the top of the axes."""
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[L, L], y=[0.02, W_RANGE[1]], mode="lines", showlegend=False, hoverinfo="skip",
                             line=dict(color=color, width=3, dash=dash)))
    fig.add_annotation(x=L, y=W_RANGE[1], text=label, showarrow=False, yanchor="bottom",
                       font=dict(color=color, size=15))
```

```{python}
def sticky_prices(Y_new=1.15, c_new=C_BAR):
    """Figs. 15.8 and 15.15: labor demand is the vertical line at the labor needed for the output demanded."""
    L0, L1 = labor_needed(Y0), labor_needed(Y_new)
    w0, w1 = supply_wage(L0), supply_wage(L1, c_new)
    demand_moves, supply_moves = abs(Y_new - Y0) > 0.001, abs(c_new - C_BAR) > 0.001
    d_label = "L<sup>d</sup>′" if demand_moves else "L<sup>d</sup>"
    s_label = "L<sup>s</sup>′" if supply_moves else "L<sup>s</sup>"
    fig = go.Figure()
    add_vertical(fig, L1, d_label, BLUE)
    if demand_moves:
        add_vertical(fig, L0, "L<sup>d</sup>" if abs(L1 - L0) > 0.1 else "", GRAY, "dash")
    end = add_curve(fig, L_GRID, supply_wage(L_GRID, c_new), s_label, TEAL)
    if supply_moves:
        add_curve(fig, L_GRID, supply_wage(L_GRID), "L<sup>s</sup>", GRAY, "dash", avoid=end)
    add_point(fig, L0, w0, "A")
    if demand_moves or supply_moves:
        add_point(fig, L1, w1, "B", where="bottom right")     # below-right of B no curve passes
        add_arrow(fig, L0, 0.05, L1, 0.05)
        add_arrow(fig, 0.05, w0, 0.05, w1)
    title = f"Output {Y0:.2f} → {Y_new:.2f}: employment {L0:.2f} → {L1:.2f}, real wage {w0:.2f} → {w1:.2f}"
    return labor_axes(fig, title, "Real wage, W/P")
```

```{python}
#| kind: widget
interact(sticky_prices,
         Y_new=FloatSlider(value=1.15, min=0.8, max=1.3, step=0.05, description="output demanded Y′", style=WIDE),
         c_new=FloatSlider(value=0.6, min=0.4, max=0.7, step=0.05, description="consumption c′", style=WIDE));
```

```{python}
#| kind: website
# @title Website version: Fig. 8 with a precomputed slider for the output demanded
slider_figure(sticky_prices, "Y_new", [0.9, 1.0, 1.05, 1.1, 1.15, 1.2, 1.3], start=1.15, label="output demanded Y′")
```

**Source.** Adapted from Fig. 15.8 in Jones (2024), [*Macroeconomics*, 6th ed.](https://wwnorton.com/books/9781324063612)

**What to notice.**

- Output demanded rises by 15 percent, employment from 1.00 to 1.23 and the real wage from 0.67 to 0.82.
- Employment and the real wage now move in the **same** direction, as they do over the business cycle. That is
  why models with sticky prices and monetary shocks, the **new Keynesian** models, became so important. Together
  with TFP shocks, they are the two "flavors" that modern DSGE models combine.
- Employment rises more than output (by the power 3/2), because each extra worker adds less output than the last.

#### Textbook Figs. 15.9, 15.10 and 15.13: monetary and financial shocks in the Smets–Wouters model

A full DSGE model reports **impulse response functions**: how one variable, such as GDP, responds over time to
one shock, such as a rise in the fed funds rate. Textbook Figs. 15.9, 15.10 and 15.13 show such responses from
the estimated model of Smets and Wouters, "Shocks and Frictions in U.S. Business Cycles: A Bayesian DSGE
Approach," *American Economic Review* 97(3), 2007, pp. 586–606
([doi:10.1257/aer.97.3.586](https://doi.org/10.1257/aer.97.3.586)). They are not recomputed here: they are the
solution of a model with sticky prices and wages, investment adjustment costs and many shocks, whose parameters
were estimated from U.S. data, and they cannot be rebuilt from public data series or read precisely off the page.
What the textbook reports:

- **Fig. 15.9**: the response of GDP to a temporary 1 percentage point rise in the fed funds rate. GDP is about
  0.2 percent lower in the first quarter, the peak fall of about 0.33 percent comes 3 to 4 quarters after the shock,
  and most of the effect is gone after 5 years (20 quarters).
- **Fig. 15.10**: the same shock, for GDP, consumption, hours worked and inflation. All four fall, as with sticky
  prices in Fig. 8 run in reverse. Consumption falls nearly as much as GDP, and inflation is slightly less than
  0.2 percentage points lower for about 2 years.
- **Fig. 15.13**: a financial friction shock that raises the interest rate households face by 1 percentage point
  above the fed funds rate. It looks much like a monetary policy shock, with its largest effect on consumption.

<!-- cell -->

## Good news about the future

Last, we look at news: people learn that the future will be better, raise their consumption today, and the labor market responds differently with flexible and with sticky prices.

<!-- cell -->

### Fig. 9: Good news in the DSGE model: flexible prices

**Goal.** See how news about the future changes the labor market today (textbook Exercise 1).

People learn of a discovery that will make the economy more productive in 5 years. Today nothing changes in
production, so labor demand stays put. But people expect to be richer, so by the permanent-income hypothesis they
consume more **today**: consumption rises from 0.6 to $c' = 0.7$. Richer people want more of every good,
including leisure, so labor supply shifts **up and to the left**.

The function `good_news` handles this event twice: with flexible prices it calls `labor_shock` from Fig. 3, and
with sticky prices (Fig. 10) it calls `sticky_prices` from Fig. 8. With sticky prices, firms must also
produce the extra consumption, so the output demanded rises by the same amount as consumption.

> **Python note.** A `ToggleButtons` widget shows a row of buttons, one per option; the function receives the
> text of the selected button.

```{python}
def good_news(c_new=0.7, prices="flexible"):
    """Figs. 15.14-15.15: good news raises consumption today from 0.6 to c_new."""
    if prices == "flexible":
        return labor_shock(c_new=c_new)
    return sticky_prices(Y_new=Y0 + (c_new - C_BAR), c_new=c_new)     # demand rises with consumption
```

```{python}
#| kind: widget
interact(good_news,
         c_new=FloatSlider(value=0.7, min=0.5, max=0.8, step=0.05, description="consumption after the news c′", style=WIDE),
         prices=ToggleButtons(options=["flexible", "sticky"], value="flexible", description="prices"));
```

```{python}
#| kind: website
# @title Website version: Fig. 9 with a precomputed slider for consumption
slider_figure(good_news, "c_new", [0.5, 0.6, 0.7, 0.8], start=0.7, label="consumption after the news c′")
```

**Source.** Adapted from Fig. 15.14 in Jones (2024), [*Macroeconomics*, 6th ed.](https://wwnorton.com/books/9781324063612),
which illustrates the worked solution to its Exercise 1.

**What to notice.**

- With flexible prices, the good news *lowers* employment today, from 1.00 to 0.89, and raises the real wage a
  little, from 0.67 to 0.69. People work less because they feel richer.
- Nothing about technology has changed yet: the whole effect comes through expectations and consumption, the
  forward-looking variable of the model.

### Fig. 10: Good news in the DSGE model: sticky prices

**Goal.** Compare the same good news with sticky prices (textbook Exercise 1(d)).

With sticky prices, firms supply whatever is demanded. The good news raises consumption, so firms must produce
more and need more workers: the vertical labor demand curve shifts right, from $Y_0 = 1$ to $Y' = 1.1$. At the
same time labor supply still shifts up, because people feel richer. Firms must pay a higher wage to get the
labor they need. Use the buttons to switch between the two cases.

```{python}
         c_new=FloatSlider(value=0.7, min=0.5, max=0.8, step=0.05, description="consumption after the news c′", style=WIDE),
         prices=ToggleButtons(options=["flexible", "sticky"], value="sticky", description="prices"));
```


**Source.** Adapted from Fig. 15.15 in Jones (2024), [*Macroeconomics*, 6th ed.](https://wwnorton.com/books/9781324063612),
which illustrates the worked solution to its Exercise 1.

**What to notice.**

- With sticky prices, employment *rises*, from 1.00 to 1.15, and the real wage rises a lot, from 0.67 to 0.90.
  With flexible prices (Fig. 9) employment fell to 0.89.
- The same shock moves employment in opposite directions depending on whether prices are sticky. This is why
  macroeconomists argue so much about how sticky prices really are.

## Concluding remarks

- **DSGE models** are *dynamic* (they trace the economy over time), *stochastic* (shocks hit it) and *general
  equilibrium* (prices clear the markets). Their shocks fade as impulse responses, equation (1), and adjustment
  costs delay their peak effects.
- They grew out of **real business cycle** models, which added TFP shocks to the Solow model, equation (2). TFP is
  measured as a Solow residual, equation (3); U.S. TFP growth swings a lot, but once utilization is removed,
  equation (4), it does not fall in most recessions.
- The **labor market** is a key block of every DSGE model. Labor demand and supply, equations (5) and (6), give
  employment and the wage in equation (7). With consumption taken as given, a TFP fall or a sales tax lowers
  employment and the wage together, like a recession; a rise in government purchases or good news acts through
  consumption and labor supply instead.
- **Nominal rigidities** decide how monetary policy works. With sticky wages, equation (8), an expansion raises
  employment but lowers the real wage; with sticky prices, equation (9), labor demand is vertical and an expansion
  raises both. Estimated DSGE models such as Smets–Wouters are **quantitative**: their impulse response functions
  say how much and how fast GDP, consumption, hours and inflation respond to each shock.
- The next chapter studies **consumption** itself: the permanent-income hypothesis and the microfoundations behind
  the consumption that this chapter took as given.
- For an advanced treatment, [Appendix H](https://quarcs-lab.github.io/macro102-site/notebooks/appH-the-dsge-model-of-smets-and-wouters.html)
  solves the full Smets–Wouters model in Python and recomputes the impulse responses of textbook Figs. 15.9–15.13.

### Conceptual problems

<!-- cell -->

**Problem 1 (Basic): How long do shocks last in an estimated DSGE model?** Smets and Wouters (2007) estimated
their model on quarterly U.S. data from 1966 to 2004. Each of its shocks fades like the shock process of the Model
overview, $x_{t+1} = \rho\,x_t + \varepsilon_{t+1}$. The table lists five of their estimates of $\rho$ (the posterior
modes in Table 1b of the [working-paper version](https://www.ecb.europa.eu/pub/pdf/scpwps/ecbwp722.pdf); the article
is [doi:10.1257/aer.97.3.586](https://doi.org/10.1257/aer.97.3.586)).

| Shock | What it moves | $\rho$ per quarter |
|---|---|---|
| productivity | TFP | 0.95 |
| government spending | public purchases | 0.97 |
| investment technology | how much new capital each dollar of investment buys | 0.71 |
| risk premium | the gap between the central bank's rate and the return households require | 0.18 |
| monetary policy | the interest rate, beyond what the central bank's rule prescribes | 0.12 |

(a) Use the half-life formula of the Model overview to compute the half-life of each shock, in quarters.

(b) Use equation (1) to compute the share of each shock that is still left one year (4 quarters) after it hits.

(c) The monetary policy shock is almost gone after a single quarter, yet the chapter reports that GDP falls most 3 to
4 quarters after a monetary shock. Which features of a DSGE model can give a short-lived shock long-lived effects?

<details><summary>Hint</summary>

The half-life is $h = \ln 2/(-\ln\rho)$, and by equation (1) the share left after $n$ quarters is $\rho^n$;
`np.log` gives the natural log. For (c), reread the frictions in "The building blocks of a DSGE model", the adjustment-cost rule
after equation (1), and ask how a central bank moves its interest rate from one quarter to the next.

</details>

<!-- cell -->

**Your answer:**

```{python}
# Your answer here
```

<details><summary>Solution</summary>

**(a) and (b).** For productivity, $h = \ln 2/(-\ln 0.95) = 0.6931/0.0513 = 13.5$ quarters, and after a year
$0.95^4 = 0.81$ of the shock is left. The same two steps for every shock give:

| Shock | $\rho$ | Half-life, quarters | Share left after a year, $\rho^4$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| productivity | 0.95 | 13.5, about 3.4 years | 0.81 |
| government spending | 0.97 | 22.8, about 5.7 years | 0.89 |
| investment technology | 0.71 | 2.0 | 0.25 |
| risk premium | 0.18 | 0.40 | 0.001 |
| monetary policy | 0.12 | 0.33 | 0.0002 |

The productivity estimate of 0.95 is close to the $\rho = 0.958$ that the Model overview derived from a half-life of
16 quarters. In Python:

```python
shocks = {"productivity": 0.95, "government spending": 0.97, "investment technology": 0.71,
          "risk premium": 0.18, "monetary policy": 0.12}
for name, rho_shock in shocks.items():
    half_life = np.log(2) / -np.log(rho_shock)
    print(f"{name:22s} half-life {half_life:5.2f} quarters, left after a year {rho_shock ** 4:.4f}")
```

`shocks.items()` walks through the pairs of a dictionary, one name and one value at a time.

**(c)** A shock and its effects are not the same thing. Three features spread a short shock over many quarters:

- **Adjustment costs.** With the rule $y_t = y_{t-1} + \lambda(x_t - y_{t-1})$, the economy closes only part of the
  gap each quarter, so its response keeps growing after the shock has faded. With $\rho = 0.8$ and $\lambda = 0.3$
  it peaks 3 quarters later (the Model overview's check).
- **Sticky prices and wages.** Prices adjust slowly, so a higher nominal interest rate is also a higher real rate for
  several quarters, and spending stays low.
- **A smooth policy rule.** In the estimated rule the interest rate puts a weight of 0.81 on its own value of the
  quarter before (Table 1a of the same paper), so a rate that jumps comes back down only slowly, long after the
  shock itself is gone.

So the long swings of a DSGE model come either from shocks that are very persistent themselves (productivity,
government spending) or from frictions that stretch short-lived shocks, like the monetary one, over many quarters.

</details>

<!-- cell -->

**Problem 2 (Intermediate): Two recessions, two stories: 1974 and 1982.** John Fernald's data in `tfp_annual.csv`
([Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco](https://www.frbsf.org/research-and-insights/data-and-indicators/total-factor-productivity-tfp/))
give, for the U.S. business sector (percent per year):

| Year | Output growth | Raw Solow residual | Utilization |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1974 | −1.56 | −3.72 | −2.62 |
| 1982 | −2.31 | −2.76 | −2.94 |

(a) Use equation (4) to compute true TFP growth in each year.

(b) In 1973–74 an oil embargo nearly quadrupled the price of oil, from \$2.90 to \$11.65 a barrel
([Federal Reserve History](https://www.federalreservehistory.org/essays/oil-shock-of-1973-74)). Our production function
has no oil in it. Explain why a jump in the price of oil can act like a fall in $\bar{A}$, and use the table
"Which way do employment and the real wage move?" of the Model overview to say what the flexible-price labor market
predicts.

(c) In 1981–82 the Federal Reserve tightened money until the federal funds rate approached 20 percent, and
unemployment reached nearly 11 percent late in 1982
([Federal Reserve History](https://www.federalreservehistory.org/essays/recession-of-1981-82)). Which row of the same
table fits 1982? Why did the raw Solow residual fall that year anyway?

(d) What do the two years say about the claim that TFP shocks drive business cycles?

<details><summary>Hint</summary>

Equation (4) says raw residual = true TFP growth + utilization growth, so subtract. For (b), think about what the same
workers and machines can produce once energy is much more expensive. For (c), a monetary contraction is a monetary
expansion run in reverse; which friction lets money change employment?

</details>

<!-- cell -->

**Your answer:**

<!-- cell -->

<details><summary>Solution</summary>

**(a)** From equation (4), $g_A = (\text{raw residual}) - g_u$:

- 1974: $g_A = -3.72 - (-2.62) = -1.10$ percent (Fernald's adjusted series has $-1.09$; the identity holds only
  approximately for annual averages);
- 1982: $g_A = -2.76 - (-2.94) = +0.18$ percent.

True TFP fell in 1974 and was roughly flat in 1982, although the raw residual fell in both years.

**(b)** Output in equation (2) is value added: what capital and labor produce beyond the materials and energy that firms
buy. When oil costs nearly four times as much, firms use less of it and switch to slower, less energy-intensive ways of
working, and some energy-hungry machines stop paying their way. The same $K$ and $L$ then produce less value added,
which the model reads as a lower $\bar{A}$. With flexible prices, labor demand shifts down: employment and the real
wage both fall, the first row of the table. This is the real business cycle story, and in 1974 it fits: true TFP fell
by about 1.1 percent in a recession year.

**(c)** A monetary contraction with **sticky prices**: the output demanded falls, the vertical labor demand curve of
equation (9) shifts left, and employment and the real wage both fall (the "monetary expansion, sticky prices" row, in
reverse). The sticky-wage row, run in reverse, fits as well: with nominal wages stuck, a lower price level raises the
real wage $\bar{W}/P$, and firms hire fewer workers. Either way a nominal rigidity lets money cut employment, and TFP
plays no role. The raw residual fell by 2.76 percent only because utilization fell by 2.94 percent:
firms kept workers and machines on hand but ran them less intensively, and equation (3) counts that as lost
productivity.

**(d)** The evidence is mixed. Some recessions, like 1974, come with a true fall in TFP; others, like 1982, have flat
TFP and a clear monetary cause. Measured with the raw residual, both years look like TFP recessions, which is why
the first RBC models looked so successful. A model of the cycle needs both TFP shocks and monetary shocks with
nominal rigidities: the two flavors that modern DSGE models combine.

</details>

<!-- cell -->

**Problem 3 (Challenge): How elastic must labor supply be?** Economists measure how strongly hours respond to a
temporary change in the wage, holding consumption fixed, with the **Frisch elasticity** $\eta$. Chetty, Guren, Manoli
and Weber ([NBER Working Paper 16729](https://www.nber.org/papers/w16729)) note that business-cycle models need much
larger labor supply elasticities than studies of individual workers find; their synthesis of the micro evidence points
to Frisch elasticities of about 0.5 for the hours of people who work and 0.25 for the decision to work at all.

(a) Show that the labor supply curve (6) has a Frisch elasticity of 1.

(b) Replace the disutility of work in the household's utility by $\frac{\eta}{\eta+1}\,\bar{\ell}^{-1/\eta}L^{(\eta+1)/\eta}$.
Derive the new labor supply curve and check that it is equation (6) when $\eta = 1$. Then solve the labor market with
labor demand (5) and no tax, and show that the elasticity of $L^*$ with respect to $\bar{A}$ is $3\eta/(3+\eta)$.

(c) In Fernald's data for 1950–2025, the growth of hours worked has a standard deviation of 2.57 percentage points
and the growth of utilization-adjusted TFP one of 1.40 points (files `tfp_inputs.csv` and `tfp_annual.csv`, from the
[Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco](https://www.frbsf.org/research-and-insights/data-and-indicators/total-factor-productivity-tfp/)).
If TFP shocks in the flexible-price labor market were the only reason hours move, how large would $\eta$ have to be?
Compare it with the micro estimate of 0.5 and with the chapter's $\eta = 1$.

<details><summary>Hint</summary>

(a) Take logs of equation (6) and change $\ln w$ with $c$ fixed. (b) The derivative of the new disutility with
respect to $L$ is $(L/\bar{\ell})^{1/\eta}$; set it equal to $w/c$. Then repeat steps 1–4 of the labor market's
"Solving the model", with the power $1/\eta$ in place of 1. (c) If $\ln L$ always moves $\epsilon$ times as much as
$\ln\bar{A}$, its standard deviation is $\epsilon$ times as large. Solve $3\eta/(3+\eta) = \epsilon$ for $\eta$.

</details>

<!-- cell -->

**Your answer:**

```{python}
# Your answer here
```

<details><summary>Solution</summary>

**(a)** Taking logs of (6), $\ln L^s = \ln\bar{\ell} + \ln w - \ln c$. With $c$ fixed, a 1 percent higher wage raises
$\ln L^s$ by 1 percent: $\partial\ln L^s/\partial\ln w = 1$, so the Frisch elasticity is 1.

**(b)** Utility is now $U = \ln c - \frac{\eta}{\eta+1}\bar{\ell}^{-1/\eta}L^{(\eta+1)/\eta}$, with $c = wL - \bar{S}$.
The power rule brings down $(\eta+1)/\eta$, which cancels the factor in front, and lowers the power by one, to
$1/\eta$:

$$\frac{dU}{dL} = \frac{w}{c} - \bar{\ell}^{-1/\eta}L^{1/\eta} = \frac{w}{c} - \left(\frac{L}{\bar{\ell}}\right)^{1/\eta} = 0
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad L^s = \bar{\ell}\left(\frac{w}{c}\right)^{\eta}.$$

With $\eta = 1$ the disutility is $\frac{1}{2}\bar{\ell}^{-1}L^2$ and $L^s = \bar{\ell}\,w/c$: equation (6). Written as a
wage, supply is $w = c\,(L/\bar{\ell})^{1/\eta}$. Set it equal to labor demand (5):

$$c\,\bar{\ell}^{-1/\eta}L^{1/\eta} = \frac{2}{3}\cdot\frac{\bar{A}K^{1/3}}{L^{1/3}}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad L^{1/\eta + 1/3} = \frac{2}{3}\cdot\frac{\bar{A}K^{1/3}\,\bar{\ell}^{1/\eta}}{c}.$$

The power on the left is $\frac{1}{\eta} + \frac{1}{3} = \frac{3+\eta}{3\eta}$, so raise both sides to $\frac{3\eta}{3+\eta}$:

$$L^* = \left[\frac{2}{3}\cdot\frac{\bar{A}K^{1/3}\,\bar{\ell}^{1/\eta}}{c}\right]^{3\eta/(3+\eta)}.$$

In logs, $\ln L^* = \text{const} + \frac{3\eta}{3+\eta}\ln\bar{A}$: the elasticity is $3\eta/(3+\eta)$, which is $3/4$
for $\eta = 1$, as in the comparative-statics table. It is 0.429 for $\eta = 0.5$ and 1.5 for $\eta = 3$, and it can never
reach 3, however elastic labor supply is: the falling marginal product caps it.

**(c)** The required elasticity is $\epsilon = 2.57/1.40 = 1.84$. Solving $3\eta/(3+\eta) = \epsilon$ gives
$3\eta = \epsilon(3+\eta)$, so $\eta = 3\epsilon/(3-\epsilon) = 4.7$. That is nearly ten times the micro estimate of
0.5. With $\eta = 0.5$, TFP shocks would move hours with a standard deviation of only $0.429 \times 1.40 = 0.60$
points, under a quarter of the 2.57 in the data; with the chapter's $\eta = 1$, about $0.75 \times 1.40 = 1.05$
points. Problem 4 adds a second difficulty: hours and adjusted TFP do not even move in the same direction.

```python
inputs = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "tfp_inputs.csv")
ratio = inputs.hours_growth.std() / inputs.tfp_util.std()
print(f"standard deviations: hours {inputs.hours_growth.std():.2f}, adjusted TFP {inputs.tfp_util.std():.2f}")
print(f"elasticity needed {ratio:.2f}, so eta = {3 * ratio / (3 - ratio):.1f}")
for eta in (0.5, 1.0, 3.0):
    print(f"eta = {eta}: employment elasticity {3 * eta / (3 + eta):.3f}")
```

This is the labor-supply puzzle of real business cycle models: to let TFP shocks drive hours, they need labor supply
far more elastic than studies of workers find. DSGE models answer with other shocks and with nominal rigidities.

</details>

growth with the raw Solow residual and with utilization-adjusted TFP growth. The flexible-price labor market predicts
that hours rise with TFP (an elasticity of 0.75); with sticky prices and unchanged demand, equation (9) predicts that
they fall (an elasticity of −3/2). Which prediction do the numbers support, and why do the two TFP measures disagree?

<details><summary>Hint</summary>

**Your answer:**

<!-- cell -->

<details><summary>Solution</summary>

Read the file and compute three correlations:

```python
inputs = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "tfp_inputs.csv")
print(f"hours and raw TFP:      {inputs.hours_growth.corr(inputs.tfp_solow):+.2f}")
print(f"hours and adjusted TFP: {inputs.hours_growth.corr(inputs.tfp_util):+.2f}")
print(f"hours and utilization:  {inputs.hours_growth.corr(inputs.utilization):+.2f}")
```

Hours growth has a correlation of +0.38 with the raw residual but −0.39 with adjusted TFP. Once utilization is
removed, years of fast TFP growth tend to be years in which hours *fall*. That is the sign that sticky prices predict:
when TFP rises and demand does not keep up, firms need fewer workers. Basu, Fernald and Kimball (2006),
["Are Technology Improvements Contractionary?"](https://www.aeaweb.org/articles?id=10.1257/aer.96.5.1418), reach the
same answer with careful estimates: inputs fall at first when technology improves, which fits simple sticky-price
models but not the standard RBC model.

The raw residual disagrees because it contains utilization (equation 4), and utilization rises and falls with hours:
their correlation is +0.65. Firms that hire more also run their workers and machines harder, and plain growth
accounting records the extra intensity as higher TFP.

</details>

**Problem 5 (Intermediate): Growth accounting by hand.** Fernald computes the raw Solow residual (`tfp_solow`) from the
columns of `tfp_inputs.csv`. Rebuild it yourself.

(a) Use equation (3), with the weights 1/3 and 2/3, to compute the residual in every year from output, capital and hours
growth; the notebook's `solow_residual` function works on whole columns. Compare your residual with `tfp_solow` in
2009 and 2020.

(b) Over 1950–2025, what are the correlation and the average gap between your residual and Fernald's?

(c) Fernald's formula differs from equation (3) in two ways: capital's share $\alpha$ is measured every year
(`capital_share`), and labor input also grows with **labor quality** $g_q$ (`labor_quality`), the skill and
experience mix of the hours worked: $g_A = g_Y - \alpha g_K - (1-\alpha)(g_L + g_q)$. Recompute the residual with this
formula. How large is the largest gap now?

(d) In which two years did labor quality grow fastest, and why might it jump in those years?

<details><summary>Hint</summary>

`solow_residual(inputs.gdp_growth, inputs.capital_growth, inputs.hours_growth)` returns a whole column; store it as a
new column. `inputs.year.isin([2009, 2020])` picks the two years, and `.nlargest(3, "labor_quality")` the years with
the fastest labor-quality growth. Look at hours growth in those years.

</details>

```{python}
# Your answer here
```

<details><summary>Solution</summary>

```python
inputs = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "tfp_inputs.csv")
inputs["simple"] = solow_residual(inputs.gdp_growth, inputs.capital_growth, inputs.hours_growth)
alpha = inputs.capital_share
inputs["full"] = (inputs.gdp_growth - alpha * inputs.capital_growth
                  - (1 - alpha) * (inputs.hours_growth + inputs.labor_quality))
print(inputs[inputs.year.isin([2009, 2020])][["year", "simple", "full", "tfp_solow"]].round(2).to_string(index=False))
gap = inputs.simple - inputs.tfp_solow
print(f"equation (3): correlation {inputs.simple.corr(inputs.tfp_solow):.3f}, average gap {gap.mean():.2f}")
print(f"with alpha and labor quality: largest gap {(inputs.full - inputs.tfp_solow).abs().max():.2f}")
print(inputs.nlargest(3, "labor_quality")[["year", "hours_growth", "labor_quality"]].to_string(index=False))
```

**(a)** In 2009, equation (3) gives $-3.75 - \tfrac{1}{3}\times 1.76 - \tfrac{2}{3}\times(-7.74) = +0.82$ percent with
these rounded numbers (+0.83 from the unrounded data), against Fernald's −0.15; in 2020 it gives +1.27 against −0.23.
In both deep recessions the simple formula even turns the sign.

**(b)** Over all 76 years the two residuals have a correlation of 0.988, but the simple one is on average 0.23 points
higher.

**(c)** With the measured capital share and labor quality, the residual is −0.25 in 2009 and −0.29 in 2020, and the
largest gap in any year is 0.10 points; it is not zero only because the identity is exact for quarterly data and
approximate for annual averages. Most of the average gap of (b) is labor quality: it grows by 0.38 percent a year on
average, and equation (3) leaves its contribution, $\tfrac{2}{3} \times 0.38 = 0.25$, inside TFP.

**(d)** The fastest years are 2020 (1.63 percent) and 2009 (1.19 percent), the two years in which hours fell by
about 7.7 percent. Labor quality weights each hour by what that kind of worker earns. When it jumps, the hours of
less experienced and lower-paid workers have fallen much more than the others, so the average quality of the hours
still worked rises. Without that correction, equation (3) counts the better mix of workers as higher TFP.

</details>

**Problem 6 (Challenge): Is the United States an exception?** In Fig. 1's "Beyond the United States" chart, the
[Penn World Table 11.0](https://www.rug.nl/ggdc/productivity/pwt/) TFP of the United States fell in only half of its
years of falling GDP, while most countries' TFP fell almost every time.

(a) For each of the 120 countries in `pwt_growth.csv`, compute the correlation between GDP growth and TFP growth over all
of its years, and collect the results in a table.

(b) What is the median correlation? Where does the United States rank, counting from the lowest? Which five countries
have the lowest correlations?

(c) Compute the median correlation in each region. Which region stands out?

(d) Does a high correlation show that TFP shocks cause booms and recessions? Use equation (4) and Problem 4.

<details><summary>Hint</summary>

Loop over `sorted(pwt.country.unique())`, keep one country's rows, and compute `.corr()` of its two columns; append a
small dictionary per country to a list and turn the list into a DataFrame with `pd.DataFrame(rows)`. Then
`.sort_values("r")`, `.median()` and `.groupby("region")`.

</details>

```{python}
# Your answer here
```

<!-- cell -->

**Your answer:**

<!-- cell -->

<details><summary>Solution</summary>

```python
pwt = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "pwt_growth.csv")
rows = []
for country in sorted(pwt.country.unique()):
    data = pwt[pwt.country == country]
    rows.append({"country": country, "region": data.region.iloc[0], "years": len(data),
                 "r": data.gdp_growth.corr(data.tfp_growth)})
table = pd.DataFrame(rows).sort_values("r")
us_r = table[table.country == "United States"].r.iloc[0]
print(f"median correlation {table.r.median():.2f}; United States {us_r:.2f}, "
      f"rank {(table.r < us_r).sum() + 1} of {len(table)} from the lowest")
print(table.head(5).round(2).to_string(index=False))
print(table.groupby("region").r.median().round(2).sort_values())
```

`rows.append({...})` adds one dictionary, one row of the future table, to the list. `.iloc[0]` takes the first value
of a column.

**(b)** The median correlation is 0.86: in most countries measured TFP rises and falls almost one for one with GDP. The
United States, at 0.70, ranks 15th of 120 from the lowest. The five lowest are Serbia (0.18, with only 29 years of data),
Tanzania (0.45), Colombia (0.51), Canada (0.56) and South Africa (0.59).

**(c)** North America, that is Canada and the United States, has a median of 0.63; every other region lies between
0.83 and 0.91. So the United States is unusual, but not alone: its neighbor is even lower.

**(d)** No. PWT's TFP is a raw Solow residual, and by equation (4) it contains the change in utilization. Whenever GDP
falls for any reason (less demand, tighter credit, a monetary contraction), firms use their workers and machines less
intensively, and the residual falls with GDP. The correlation can therefore run from GDP to measured TFP, not from TFP
to GDP. For the United States, the one country here with a utilization-adjusted series, Problem 4 found that adjusted
TFP and hours move in opposite directions.

</details>

> **Python note.** `fixed(C_BAR)` holds an argument at one value, so `interact` draws no slider for it.

<details><summary>Solution</summary>

The closest slider value is $\bar{A} = 1.020$. The title reads employment 1.01, a real wage of 0.68 and output 1.03:
the model predicts a **boom**, with more jobs, higher wages and more output. The functions give the exact numbers:

```python
L_2020, w_2020 = equilibrium(A=1.0181)       # the measured rise of 1.81 percent
Y_2020 = output(L_2020, 1.0181)
print(f"TFP 1.0181: employment {L_2020:.4f}, real wage {w_2020:.4f}, output {Y_2020:.4f}")
```

With $\bar{A}' = 1.0181$, employment is 1.0135, the real wage 0.6757 and output 1.0273: output rises by 2.73
percent, about 3/2 times the rise in TFP. Measured output fell by 2.90 percent, so the model misses by 5.63
percentage points, and in the wrong direction. A TFP shock cannot explain the pandemic recession: the fall in output
must have come from other shocks, to the supply of labor and to spending.

**Problem 8 (Intermediate): How large is the spending multiplier with flexible prices?** A government raises its
purchases by $\Delta G$, paid for with taxes. Households, poorer over their lifetimes, cut consumption, and as in
Fig. 5 they work more. The **multiplier** $\Delta Y/\Delta G$ is the rise in output per unit of extra purchases. The
sliders below set $\Delta G$ and the share of it that households cut from consumption: 1 for a permanent rise, less
for a temporary one.

(a) For a permanent rise of $\Delta G = 0.1$, what are employment, output and the multiplier?

(b) Keep $\Delta G = 0.1$. What is the smallest share on the slider that gives a multiplier of at least 0.8? Then
find the exact share with the output formula of (a). Is a program with that share closer to a permanent or to a
temporary rise in purchases?

(c) Ramey (2011) concludes that the multiplier for a temporary, deficit-financed rise in purchases is probably between
0.8 and 1.5 ([*Journal of Economic Literature*](https://www.aeaweb.org/articles?id=10.1257/jel.49.3.673)). Can the
flexible-price model deliver that? What would you add to it?

> **Python note.** The widget cell defines a small function that sets consumption from the two sliders, redraws
> Fig. 2's diagram with `labor_market`, and then replaces its title with `fig.update_layout(title=...)`.

<details><summary>Hint</summary>

Consumption is $c' = 0.6 - \text{share} \times \Delta G$. Output changes only through employment, because $\bar{A}$
and $K$ do not move. For (b), raise the share one step at a time and watch the multiplier in the title. For the exact
share, work backward: first the output that a multiplier of 0.8 requires, then the consumption that gives that output.

</details>

```{python}
#| kind: widget
def spending_multiplier(G_rise=0.1, share=1.0):
    """Figs. 2 and 5 again: purchases rise by G_rise and consumption falls by share x G_rise."""
    c_new = C_BAR - share * G_rise
    L_base, w_base = equilibrium()
    L_new, w_new = equilibrium(c=c_new)
    multiplier = (output(L_new) - output(L_base)) / G_rise
    fig = labor_market(c=c_new)
    fig.update_layout(title=f"Employment {L_new:.2f}, output {output(L_new):.2f}, "
                            f"multiplier ΔY/ΔG = {round(multiplier, 2) + 0.0:.2f}")
    return fig


interact(spending_multiplier,
         G_rise=FloatSlider(value=0.1, min=0.02, max=0.2, step=0.02, description="rise in purchases ΔG", style=WIDE),
         share=FloatSlider(value=1.0, min=0.0, max=1.0, step=0.1, description="share cut from consumption",
                           style=WIDE));
```

**Source.** The model of Figs. 2 and 5 above, adapted from Figs. 15.2 and 15.5 in Jones (2024), [*Macroeconomics*, 6th ed.](https://wwnorton.com/books/9781324063612)

```{python}
# Your answer here
```

<!-- cell -->

**Your answer:**

<!-- cell -->

<details><summary>Solution</summary>

```python
L_base, w_base = equilibrium()
for share in (1.0, 0.8, 0.9, 0.3):
    L_new, w_new = equilibrium(c=C_BAR - share * 0.1)
    multiplier = (output(L_new) - output(L_base)) / 0.1
    print(f"share {share}: employment {L_new:.3f}, output {output(L_new):.3f}, "
          f"multiplier {round(multiplier, 2) + 0.0:.2f}")
c_exact = C_BAR / 1.08 ** 2                  # the consumption that gives output 1.08
print(f"A multiplier of 0.8 needs c' = {c_exact:.3f}, a share of {(C_BAR - c_exact) / 0.1:.2f}")
```

**(a)** A permanent rise cuts consumption from 0.6 to 0.5. By equation (7), employment rises to
$(0.6/0.5)^{3/4} = 1.147$, and output to $(0.6/0.5)^{1/2} = 1.095$. The multiplier is $(1.095 - 1)/0.1 = 0.95$.

**(b)** On the slider, a share of 0.8 gives a multiplier of 0.74 and a share of **0.9** gives 0.85, so 0.9 is the
smallest share that reaches 0.8. Exactly: a multiplier of 0.8 needs output $1 + 0.8 \times 0.1 = 1.08$. By (a),
output is $(0.6/c')^{1/2}$, so $c' = 0.6/1.08^2 = 0.514$, and the share is $(0.6 - 0.514)/0.1 = 0.86$. Households
must cut their consumption by 86 percent of the extra purchases, almost as much as for a permanent rise. With
flexible prices, extra purchases raise output only through the wealth effect: people work more because they feel
poorer.

**(c)** No. For a temporary rise, the case Ramey studies, households lose little lifetime income, so they cut
consumption by much less than the 86 percent of (b), and the flexible-price multiplier stays far below 0.8: with a
share of 0.3 it is only 0.26, and less the shorter the program. Only a permanent, tax-financed rise gets
close to 1, and then consumption and the real wage fall. To reach a multiplier near 1 for a temporary program, add
**sticky prices**: firms then produce whatever is demanded, so the extra purchases raise output directly, as in
Fig. 8. The estimated Smets–Wouters model, which has sticky prices, finds a multiplier of about 1 (the note after
Fig. 5).

</details>

**Problem 9 (Intermediate): One employment target, two frictions.** The central bank wants a monetary expansion that
raises employment by 10 percent. How large must the expansion be, and what happens to the real wage,

(a) when nominal wages are sticky at $\bar{W} = 0.75$, as in Figs. 6–7, starting from point $A$ with employment 0.70
(the expansion raises the price level by `size` percent);

(b) when prices are sticky, as in Fig. 8, starting from $Y_0 = 1$ (the expansion raises the output demanded by `size`
percent)?

(c) Which case is better for the workers who already have a job, and which looks more like an actual boom?

Get close with the sliders, then find the exact answers with the model's equations.

<details><summary>Hint</summary>

With sticky wages, firms are on their labor demand curve, and employment grows with the cube of the price level (the
Model overview's sticky-wage block). With sticky prices, use equation (9) with $\bar{A} = K = 1$. Set each employment
ratio equal to 1.1 and solve for $P'$ and $Y'$.

</details>

```{python}
#| kind: widget
def expansion(friction="sticky wages", size=3.0):
    """Figs. 7 and 8 again: prices (sticky wages) or the output demanded (sticky prices) rise by size percent."""
    if friction == "sticky wages":
        return sticky_wages(t=1, P_new=1 + size / 100, W_bar=0.75)
    fig = sticky_prices(Y_new=1 + size / 100, c_new=C_BAR)
    for trace in fig.data:
        if trace.text == ("A",):
            trace.textposition = "top left"      # keeps the letter A clear of a nearby point B
    return fig


interact(expansion,
         friction=ToggleButtons(options=["sticky wages", "sticky prices"], value="sticky wages",
                                description="friction"),
         size=FloatSlider(value=3.0, min=2.0, max=10.0, step=0.5, readout_format=".1f",
                          description="size of the expansion (percent)", style=WIDE));
```

**Source.** The models of Figs. 7 and 8 above, adapted from Figs. 15.7 and 15.8 in Jones (2024), [*Macroeconomics*, 6th ed.](https://wwnorton.com/books/9781324063612)

```{python}
# Your answer here
```

<!-- cell -->

**Your answer:**

<!-- cell -->

<details><summary>Solution</summary>

**(a)** Along labor demand, $L^d = \left[\tfrac{2}{3}\big/(\bar{W}/P')\right]^3 = (P')^3 L^d(\bar{W})$, so employment
rises by 10 percent when $(P')^3 = 1.1$, that is $P' = 1.1^{1/3} = 1.032$: prices must rise by about 3.2 percent. On the
slider, 3 percent gives employment 0.77. The real wage falls from 0.75 to $0.75/1.032 = 0.727$, by 3.1 percent.

**(b)** By equation (9), $L = (Y')^{3/2}$, so $(Y')^{3/2} = 1.1$ gives $Y' = 1.1^{2/3} = 1.066$: the output demanded must
rise by 6.6 percent (on the slider, 6.5 percent already gives employment 1.10). The real wage lies on the supply
curve, $w = cL/\bar{\ell}$, so it rises by the same 10 percent, from 0.667 to 0.733.

```python
P_new = 1.1 ** (1 / 3)
L_A, L_B = labor_demand(0.75), labor_demand(0.75 / P_new)
print(f"Sticky wages: P' = {P_new:.4f}, employment {L_A:.3f} -> {L_B:.3f}, real wage 0.750 -> {0.75 / P_new:.3f}")
Y_new = 1.1 ** (2 / 3)
L_sticky = labor_needed(Y_new)
print(f"Sticky prices: Y' = {Y_new:.4f}, employment 1.000 -> {L_sticky:.3f}, "
      f"real wage {supply_wage(1.0):.3f} -> {supply_wage(L_sticky):.3f}")
```

**(c)** With sticky wages the new jobs are paid for by everyone who already works: their real wage falls by 3.1
percent. With sticky prices employment and the real wage rise together, by 10 percent each, as they tend to do in
actual booms. The two pushes differ in size for two reasons. Prices need to rise by only 3.2 percent because labor
demand is very elastic: firms hire about 3 percent more for each 1 percent fall in the real wage. Output demanded must
rise by 6.6 percent, two thirds of the employment gain, because $Y = L^{2/3}$: each extra worker adds less output than
the last.

</details>

**Problem 10 (Challenge): A TFP shock or a tax-like wedge in 2009?** In 2009, hours worked in the U.S. business sector
fell by 7.74 percent and output by 3.75 percent, while utilization-adjusted TFP rose by 3.53 percent (`tfp_inputs.csv`).
Chari, Kehoe and McGrattan (2007) showed that many frictions act in a growth model like time-varying **wedges** that
resemble taxes on labor or investment ([Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis staff
report](https://www.minneapolisfed.org/research/staff-reports/business-cycle-accounting); published in *Econometrica*,
[doi:10.1111/j.1468-0262.2007.00768.x](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1468-0262.2007.00768.x)). Jermann and Quadrini (2012)
find that tighter financing conditions for firms contributed to the 2008–2009 recession
([*American Economic Review*](https://www.aeaweb.org/articles?id=10.1257/aer.102.1.238)). In our labor market, the
sales tax $\tau$ is such a wedge.

(a) With the sliders, check that a TFP fall to $\bar{A}' = 0.90$ with no wedge, and a wedge $\tau = 0.10$ with TFP
unchanged, both lower employment to 0.92, close to the fall in hours of 2009.

(b) For each story, compute the change in output and the measured Solow residual of equation (3), with capital fixed,
in percent (100 times the change in the log, as in Fernald's data).

(c) Which story fits the 2009 data better?

(d) Suppose the wedge comes from expensive credit: firms must borrow to pay wages before they sell their output. Which
policies would raise employment in that case, and why would they do little against a true fall in TFP?

<details><summary>Hint</summary>

Only the product $(1-\tau)\bar{A}$ enters equation (7), but output $Y = \bar{A}K^{1/3}L^{2/3}$ contains $\bar{A}$ alone.
For (b), use `equilibrium`, `output`, `np.log` and `solow_residual(g_Y, 0.0, g_L)`.

</details>

```{python}
#| kind: widget
interact(labor_shock,
         A_new=FloatSlider(value=1.0, min=0.8, max=1.0, step=0.1, description="TFP after the shock Ā′", style=WIDE),
         tau=FloatSlider(value=0.0, min=0.0, max=0.2, step=0.1, description="tax-like wedge τ", style=WIDE),
         c_new=fixed(C_BAR));
```

**Source.** The model of Figs. 3 and 4 above, adapted from Figs. 15.3 and 15.4 in Jones (2024), [*Macroeconomics*, 6th ed.](https://wwnorton.com/books/9781324063612)

```{python}
# Your answer here
```

<!-- cell -->

**Your answer:**

<!-- cell -->

<details><summary>Solution</summary>

**(a)** In both cases $(1-\tau)\bar{A} = 0.9$, so equation (7) gives the same point: employment $0.9^{3/4} = 0.924$
and a real wage of 0.616. The title reads "Employment 1.00 → 0.92, real wage 0.67 → 0.62" for either slider.

**(b)** Output and the residual differ, because only the TFP story lowers $\bar{A}$ in the production function:

```python
for A_new, tau in [(0.9, 0.0), (1.0, 0.1)]:
    L_new, w_new = equilibrium(A=A_new, tau=tau)
    g_L = 100 * np.log(L_new)                     # percent, as 100 times the change in the log
    g_Y = 100 * np.log(output(L_new, A_new))
    residual = round(solow_residual(g_Y, 0.0, g_L), 2) + 0.0
    print(f"A = {A_new}, tau = {tau}: employment {g_L:.2f}%, output {g_Y:.2f}%, Solow residual {residual:.2f}%")
```

| Story | Employment, percent | Output, percent | Solow residual, percent |
|---|---|---|---|
| TFP falls to 0.90 | −7.90 | −15.80 | −10.54 |
| wedge $\tau = 0.10$ | −7.90 | −5.27 | 0.00 |

In the TFP story, $g_Y = g_A + \tfrac{2}{3}g_L = -10.54 + \tfrac{2}{3}\times(-7.90) \approx -15.8$. In the wedge story,
$\bar{A}$ does not change, so $g_Y = \tfrac{2}{3}g_L = -5.27$ and the residual is zero.

**(c)** The wedge story. With hours down by about 8 percent, a TFP recession would have cut output by about 16
percent and measured TFP by more than 10 percent. In 2009 output fell by 3.75 percent, the raw residual by only 0.15
percent, and adjusted TFP rose. The wedge story gets both facts roughly right: an output fall of about 5 percent
(somewhat less in the data, because capital still grew by 1.76 percent) and no fall in TFP.

**(d)** If the wedge is expensive credit, policies that make borrowing cheaper or easier lower $\tau$ and shift labor
demand back up: lower interest rates, central bank lending to banks and firms, loan guarantees, or rebuilding banks'
capital. Against a true TFP fall they would do little, because each worker really produces less: cheaper credit does
not raise the marginal product of labor, so firms would still want fewer workers at any given wage.

</details>
